# Parallel Logical Measurements via Quantum Code Surgery

Watson Research Center, Yorktown Heights, NY 10598, USA Quantum code surgery is a flexible and low-overhead technique for performing logical measurements on quantum error-correcting codes, which generalises lattice surgery. In this work, we present a code surgery scheme, applicable to any qubit stabiliser low-density parity check (LDPC) code, that fault-tolerantly measures many logical Pauli operators in parallel. This is all done in time O(d) independent of t. Our proposed scheme preserves both the LDPC property and the fault-distance of the original code, without requiring ancillary logical codeblocks which may be costly to prepare. This addresses a shortcoming of several recently introduced surgery schemes which can only be applied to measure a limited number of logical operators in parallel if they overlap on data qubits.

Topological codes, specifically surface codes, have long been the leading candidates for the practical implementation of large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computation. Recently, experiments have demonstrated sub-threshold scaling of surface codes [1, 2] and logical operations on 2D color codes [3–5]. Despite their many desirable properties, topological codes in flat space have a notable limitation: their low encoding rate leads to a significant space overhead in achieving fault tolerance. This limitation motivates the study of quantum Low-Density Parity Check (LDPC) codes (see Ref. [6] for a recent review), which have higher rate and therefore serve as candidates for low-overhead fault-tolerant

For topological codes, particularly surface codes [9], methods for logical computation are well-studied [10–12]. Quantum LDPC codes, however, require new techniques to perform logical computation. Several methods have been proposed, such as constructing codes with native transversal gates [13–25], homomorphic logical measurements [26, 27], and generalised surgery [28]. Transversal gates can in principle be performed in constant time [29, 30] and with no additional overhead on the quantum code given a sufficiently Alexander Cowtan: akcowtan@gmail.com

Each timestep contains logically disjoint Pauli products, meaning that they act on different logical qubits, see Def. 1.2. The logically disjoint Pauli products are measured in parallel. powerful decoder, but cannot be universal by the Eastin-Knill theorem [31], and also require a quantum code to have particular structure.1 Homomorphic measurements and generalised code surgery (also known as LDPC code surgery or simply code surgery) are both techniques that perform logical Pauli measurements on logical qubits, which makes them well-suited to Pauli-based computation [33] where Pauli measurements and magic states together enable universal quantum computation.2 Nonetheless, homomorphic logical measurements are, thus far, restricted to topological codes and homological product codes. By contrast, generalised code surgery is applicable to any LDPC code.3 To perform code surgery, we initialise an ancilla system, consisting of new qubits and stabiliser generators, to deform the quantum code in such a way that chosen logical operators are decomposed into stabilisers, a procedure that can be viewed as gauge-fixing or weight reduction [28, 35–40]. Code surgery performs a logical measurement on the decomposed operators, which can be made fault-tolerant by measuring all of the new stabiliser generators for a sufficient number of rounds (typically taken to be the code distance d) to prevent timelike errors. After obtaining the logical measurement outcome, we then measure out the ancillary qubits and return to the original code. In this work, we present a code surgery scheme that performs parallel measurements of logical Pauli operators, applicable to any LDPC codes. For a collection of logically disjoint Pauli product measurements (see Def. 1.2 and Fig. 1) supported on t logical qubits, our

tω(logt + log3 ω) ) ancilla qubits, where ω≥ d is the maximum weight of the single logical Pauli representatives involved in the measurements. This provides access to a wide array of parallel logical operations which can be complemented by transversal magic gates or magic state preparation to achieve universal fault-tolerant quantum computation.

code surgery was first investigated by Cohen et al. [28] using Tanner graphs, with a space overhead of O(ωd)≥ O(d2) per logical qubit to be measured, given logical operator representatives with weight ω. This space overhead was required to guarantee fault tolerance. We call this the CKBB scheme from now on. Cowtan & Burton [41] took a different approach, using homology, yielding a similar construction where fault tolerance is not guaranteed but the overhead is reduced. This was found to be sufficient to preserve the distance in small practical cases [42]. Shortly after Ref. [42], the independent work of Cross et al. [43] showed that if the measured logical operators have suitable expansion properties, then the overhead of the CKBB scheme can be qualitatively reduced without a guarantee that the deformed code is LDPC. Later, Ide et al. [40] and Williamson & Yoder [39] independently proposed that one can directly construct an ancilla system with sufficient expansion (instead of relying on the existing expansion properties of the operators) to measure an arbitrary Pauli logical operator with space overheadO(ω log3 ω), where the log3 ω factor comes from graph decongestion [44] and the deformed code remains

Remark 1.1. More precisely, the decongestion overhead was not discussed in Ref. [40], beyond stating that it is polylogarithmic, as they found that in practice it was not required for the codes of interest. In the first arXiv preprint version of Ref. [39] it was erroneously claimed that the decongestion overhead was O(log2 ω). Performing Pauli product measurements of disjoint logical operators was further improved by using adapters to connect their ancilla systems in Swaroop et al. [45], building on earlier ideas of bridging from Ref. [43] and applying the gauging measurement directly to disjoint logical operators in Ref. [39]. In summary, current methods require O(rω log3 ω) ancillary qubits to measure the product of r logical Pauli operators that are disjoint on the physical data qubits. Unfortunately, while there have been vast improvements to the original O(dω) overhead of the CKBB scheme, parallelisation has presented a persistent obstacle. This obstacle is present because, generically, the logical operators to be measured in a high-rate LDPC code overlap substantially on data qubits as in Figure 2(b), with the overlap growing with the rate and distance of the code. Consequently, deforming a code without drastically increasing stabiliser weights or stabiliser overlap, and thereby losing the LDPC property,

To address the parallelisation challenge, Zhang & Li [46] proposed techniques called brute-force branching and devised sticking, such that logical operators of the same type, say ̄Z Pauli product measurements, can be measured in parallel using a single ancilla system. At a high level, brute-force branching uses branching stickers to create new, disjoint representatives of logical operators on ancilla qubits, which are then measured using the CKBB scheme. Devised sticking, on the other hand, measures all logical operators in a region of the code at once using the CKBB scheme, but requires additional checks and qubits to avoid measuring unwanted logical operators. Zhang & Li’s techniques have three main limitations: (a) they use the CKBB scheme for measurement, which leads to worst-case space overheads of O(tω(logt+d)) and O(t2ωd) for measurement by brute-force branching and devised sticking respectively, both of which are at least quadratic in d as ω ≥ d 4. (b) Their scheme cannot measure operators 4Note that even if ω∈ O(n), d will be asymptotically much larger than log3 ω unless d is exponentially smaller than n. Thus when taking the same logical representatives as input, our scheme is asymptotically more efficient than Zhang & Li in most reasonable cases, with hyperbolic surface codes a notable

containing Y terms in parallel without using ancillary logical|Y⟩ states, as proposed by Ref. [48, Fig. 10] in the context of twist-free lattice surgery. To prepare these logical|Y⟩ states, Zhang & Li required that the LDPC code used must support a transversal logical S gate which is a non-trivial assumption. Distillation, as an alternative, would be much more costly. Moreover, even to measure operators containing a mixture ofX andZ terms in parallel Zhang & Li required ancillary logical|0⟩ states. (c) Their scheme is specific to Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes, rather than more general stabiliser codes.

Our surgery scheme features two important improvements. First of all, we use the gauging measurement scheme of Ref. [39] instead of the CKBB scheme, which leads to a significantly lower space overhead and more rigorous guarantees on fault tolerance. Secondly, we consider the problem of measuring a logically disjoint collection of Pauli product operators,

A logical Pauli product operator P is simply a product of these single logical qubit operators, up to multiplication by stabilisers. The logical support of P is the set of logical qubits on which P acts non-trivially. A collection of logical Pauli product operators P1,··· ,Pl is logically disjoint if their logical

Intuitively, logically disjoint Pauli product operators act on different logical qubits, i.e. there is no overlap in the logical qubit support. For example, ̄X1⊗ ̄Z2 and ̄Z3⊗ ̄X4, as shown in the first timestep of Fig. 1, are logically disjoint, but ̄X1 ⊗ ̄Z2 and ̄Z2 ⊗ ̄Z3, shown in timesteps 1 and 2 respectively, are not. Logically disjoint Pauli product operators need not act on different physical qubits, and the physical qubit supports may overlap substantially. Our scheme can measure logically disjoint mixed type operators that contain logical Y terms in parallel without using ancilla|Y⟩ states or codeblocks. This is a stronger result than the scheme for measuring operators of the same type (X or Z) introduced in Ref. [46]. In the same vein, our scheme can also measure logical operators in parallel on stabiliser codes which are not CSS. We combine several elements from the recent literature to obtain our results. First, we use a particular basis [49, Sec. 4.1] and a generalised version of brute-force branching from Ref. [46] to obtain copies of the logicals to be measured. Then we construct ancillary expander graphs for each measurement, following Refs. [39, 40], and use the adapters from Ref. [45] to connect the ancillary systems to generate product measurements. At a high level, the overall space overhead of our scheme comes from the fact that brute-force branching t logicals, with weight up to ω each, costs O(tω logt), and then measurement requires a further O(tω log3 ω). In that extension, the scheme is no longer logical ancilla-free, but all the remaining rows in Fig. 3 are identical. Remark 1.3 (Weights of logical representatives). Existing methods of LDPC code surgery deform the local code around logical representatives, hence the cost in terms of additional qubits and checks is reliant on the choice of representatives and their weights.

While there are codes for which such Pauli representatives can always be chosen to have weight d, or weights bounded by O(d) as the blocklength increases, this is not true in general. 3D toric codes, for example, have ̄X logical operators which are asymptotically

As a consequence, to be fully general, our costs must be computed in terms of ω, the largest logical representative weight of the Paulis to be measured, rather than d. Furthermore, our surgery scheme requires the logical operator representatives ̄X1,··· , ̄Xk and ̄Z1,··· , ̄Zk to satisfy a set of conditions regarding their supports. While such a basis always exists in any stabiliser code [49], these representatives could have weights that are asymptotically far larger than d, bounded by O(n) in general. This is unsurprising, as we require no additional structure of the LDPC code which we are performing code surgery on, and good quantum LDPC codes are known to exist [55], hence the logical representative weights to be measured cannot be bounded in general by anything less than O(n).

First, we assume that we can modify the qubit connectivity between rounds of logical measurements, so we can initialise new ancilla systems with very different connectivity for each round of logical measurements without concern. This is different from the setting of Refs. [43, 56, 57], in which ancilla systems with fixed connectivity are constructed that can be toggled to measure different serialised Pauli products. Second, we focus on the asymptotic regime, rather than considering finite-size codes with specific (pseudo-)thresholds. For finite-size codes, we expect that our procedure can be substantially optimised to reduce the overhead far below what the asymptotic upper bound indicates, following Refs. [42, 43]. For example, it has been found that a variety of near-term codes do not require decongestion of the expander graphs used for measurement [39,40]. Furthermore, while brute-force branching is asymptotically efficient, the constant factor overheads are formidable and so minimising the branching cost is vital for our scheme to be efficient on low-blocklength codes. We leave such numerical optimisation to future work. Third, the noise model we consider in our notion of fault tolerance is a phenomenological Pauli and measurement noise model, where Pauli faults may occur on data qubits or measurement outcomes. The phenomenological noise model is justified in Appendix D.

2.1 Stabiliser codes and Tanner graphs Here we introduce some basic definitions and lemmas, which are used later. Definition 2.1. Let Pn be the Pauli group over n qubits. A qubit stabiliser code Q is specified by an Abelian subgroup S ⊂ Pn such that the codespace H is the mutual +1

A qubit CSS code Q is a qubit stabiliser code where the generators of S can be split into two sets SX and SZ. SX contains Pauli products with terms drawn from {X,I} and SZ terms drawn from{Z,I}. Thus there is a stabiliser check matrix H for Q such that

Definition 2.3. A low-density parity check (LDPC) code family is an infinite family of stabiliser codes such that the number of qubits participating in each check operator and the number of stabiliser checks that each qubit participates in are both upper-bounded by a

Logical operators in a stabiliser code are Pauli products that commute with all the checks of the code. As the stabiliser group is Abelian, all stabilisers are equivalent to the trivial logical operator. The code distance d of Q is the minimum Pauli weight of all the nontrivial logical operator representatives. We can use Tanner graphs to describe stabiliser codes, see Figure 4. Definition 2.4. A Tanner graph is a bipartite graph with a vertex for each qubit and each check. A qubit is connected to each check in which it participates with an edge labeled [1|0], [0|1], or [1|1] depending on whether the check acts on the qubit as X, Z, or Y . In our convention, data qubits are black circles and checks are boxes. If a check only measures Z or X terms then we omit the edge label, and instead label the box with a Z or X. Therefore for a CSS code we have no edge labels, and all boxes contain either Z or X labels. In this case, the condition that all stabilisers commute is the same as saying that the number of paths between every Z and X check is even.

Qubits are gathered into disjoint named sets Q0, Q1, Q2,..., and the same for checks C0, C1, C2,... . An edge between Qi and Cj is then labeled with the stabiliser check matrix of Q restricted to Qi and lifted to Cj, so we have

See Appendix A.1 for a concise summary of hypergraph product codes. We use Tanner graphs, particularly scalable Tanner graphs, extensively to describe our procedures. Throughout this work, we build on prior literature on quantum LDPC code surgery. We now recount relevant elements that we use.

Brute-force branching is a method for separating logical operators into new, disjoint supports on the leaves of a tree, see Figure 6. These new operators are equivalent to the original, but are more convenient for performing logical measurements [46] without losing the LDPC property. After logical measurements, the branches are removed by measuring them out. Branching does not perform any logical operation on the code. Brute-force branching is formally defined as follows: letQ be a CSS code. Let I ={vi : i∈ 1, 2,...,t} be a set of ̄Z logicals with support on some data qubits, and let V = ⋃ ivi be the union of those supports. Any logical can overlap with any other, and there may be other logicals J with support wholly in V other than the vi logicals. 5Terminology borrowed from Ref. [58].

Figure 6: Illustration of brute-force branching logical representatives with overlapping support. A brute-force branching of V is then a tree, which we always take to be a binary tree, of small hypergraph product patches, called branching stickers, connected to V in such a manner as to separate all the logicals vi into disjoint supports. V is then the root of the tree, and each leaf contains a copy of each vi. Brute-force branching can be described by a scalable Tanner graph, as shown in Figure 7. Explicitly, let T (Q) be the Tanner graph of Q. Let|I| = t. Take⌈t 2 ⌉ of the logicals in I and let the union of their supports on data qubits be S1. Let the set of all X-checks incident to S1 be χ1. Including the edges E1 between S1 and χ1, these generate a bipartite subgraph G1(S1 ∪χ1,E1) of the Tanner graph of Q. Then introduce a new graphG⊺ 1(S⊺ 1 ∪χ⊺ 1,E1). This graph has the same vertices and edges asG1, but each vertex in S⊺ 1 is a Z-check, rather than a data qubit, and each vertex in χ⊺ 1 is a data qubit, rather than an X-check. Connect G⊺ 1(S⊺ 1 ∪χ⊺ 1,E1) to the original Tanner graph of Q by the introduction of edges (u,u′) for u∈S1 and its corresponding u′∈S⊺ 1 for each u, and the same for v∈ χ1 and v′ ∈ χ⊺ 1. Now introduce another new graph H1, which is a copy of G1. Connect H1 to G⊺ 1 via edges (u′,u) for each u′∈S⊺ 1 and (v′,v) for each v∈χ⊺ 1. Thus far, we have created a single branch for⌈t 2 ⌉ of the logicals in I. The creation of this single branch can be viewed as gluing a hypergraph product code, see Fig. 5(c), to the code Q. Repeat this procedure for the other⌊t 2 ⌋ logicals: given the union of their supports on data qubits S2 and χ2, all X-checks incident to S2, construct G⊺ 2(S⊺ 2 ∪χ⊺ 2,E2), connect it in a 1-to-1 fashion, then construct H2 and connect it to G⊺ 2 in a 1-to-1 fashion.6 Repeat this process O(logt) times until we have our t logicals on different stickers on the leaves of the tree. Each leaf corresponds to an equivalent copy of a logical vi ∈ I. Hence all t logicals have disjoint support, and we have preserved the LDPC property. If the initial logicals had maximum representative weight ω then each level of the tree uses O(tω) qubits and checks, so the number of additional qubits and checks required for branching will be at most O(tω logt). Of course, if there are logicals in V which have no overlap with any other logicals vi , they do not need to be brute-force branched and can be measured directly. If the initial code Q has a basis of logical operators of both ̄Z and ̄X type which are disjoint where they commute, as with e.g. disjoint surface code patches, then brute-force branching is 6Throughout this paper the branching ancillary system has 1-to-1 connections from the first layer of a branch to the appropriate subset of logicals being branched. In Ref. [46] this is left as a variable, so one can choose this connectivity.

In Appendix B we demonstrate branching in detail on toy examples. Lemma 2.5. Brute-force branching creates a new representative on each leaf for each vi ∈ I, and introduces no new logical operators. Proof. Here we give a proof sketch for readers familiar with the CKBB scheme [28]. In Appendix A.2 we introduce a new perspective on brute-force branching as a series of mapping cylinders. This provides an algebraic and formal proof, but which requires some knowledge of elementary homological algebra. For each vi ∈ I, consider the path P down the binary tree from the root to its corresponding leaf. Multiplyvi by theZ checks connected to data qubits invi on the first layer, on the branch in the path P . As vi is a logical operator, this product of Z checks leaves no support in layer 1, and cleansvi to one of the branches in layer 2. Continue this procedure alongP , until all support has been moved to the leaf corresponding tovi. This logical is then another representative of the same operator as vi. When measuring ̄Z logicals in the CKBB scheme, operators corresponding to new logical qubits (gauge logicals) appear precisely at every odd layer of the attached Tanner graph, that is Z layers [28]. Let ∂1 be the local code of ̄Z logicals and incident X checks. Then, in the CKBB scheme, the data qubits on odd layers and their incident Z checks form a code ∂⊺ 1 . As ker(∂⊺ 1 )̸= 0 in general, these can form new gauge ̄X logicals, and indeed these are the only new logicals that can appear, other than their anticommuting

When performing brute-force branching, all these new gauge logicals are actually stabilisers. For any new gauge logicalg in an odd layerl, apply the correspondingX checks in layerl + 1. This creates no newX support on layerl + 1, asg∈ ker(∂ ⊺ 1 ) by definition, but does create someX support on layerl +2. This newX operator must also not violate any Z checks on this layer, as it is a product of a logical and a stabiliser. Continue applying X checks until the last layer, at which point there are no new layers upon which to add X support, and hence the gauge logical was a product of X checks, and so a stabiliser. This proof is essentially a cleaning argument, cf. Ref. [60, Lem. 1]. Remark 2.6. As a consequence of Lemma 2.5, unlike in the CKBB measurement scheme, we do not have to move to a subsystem code when brute-force branching. The CKBB measurement scheme for a ̄Z operator ends with a layer ofZ-checks, rather than a layer of X-checks when brute-force branching, which leads to gauge operators which are inequivalent

Lemma 2.7. [46, Thm. 2] Brute-force branching cannot reduce the code distance. Proof. Assume we are branching ̄Z logicals w.l.o.g. on a starting code Q with distance d. As there are no new logical qubits, to prove that the code distance is preserved we only need to show that multiplying old logicals in the starting code by stabilisers in the new code does not reduce the distance. For theX distance, observe that all newX checks are on new data qubits, but there are oldX checks which have been deformed to have support on the first layer of the branching. Applying these old X checks cannot reduce the weight of an initial ̄X operator’s support on Q below d, as it only has new support on new qubits. In other words, if we take an operator ̄ΛX on Q and apply deformed checks CD, the restriction of CD ̄ΛX to Q must have weight at leastd. The newX checks only have support on new qubits, and so cannot reduce the weight of any operator on Q. Therefore the X distance is at least d.

For the Z distance, we start with an arbitrary operator ̄ΛZ on Q. Applying a new Z check in the first layer moves the support of ̄ΛZ from support of the check in Q to their matching data qubits in the second layer of that branch, which is an X layer, potentially leaving behind more support in Q and on the first layer. We can repeat this process, but there are always X layers after every Z layer so we always add more support, and so the weight of ̄ΛZ cannot be decreased, hence the Z distance is at least d. Remark 2.8. The reason why the CKBB scheme [28] requires O(d) layers to preserve the distance, rather than only 2 layers for each branch when brute-force branching, is also because in the CKBB measurement scheme for a ̄Z operator, we end with a Z layer rather

To perform brute-force branching of ̄Z logicals, we initialise all new qubits in the|+⟩ basis at the same time and then measure all checks. For ̄X logicals, the scheme is dualised and we initialise in the|0⟩ basis instead. Lemma 2.9. Brute-force branching is a fault-tolerant operation with fault-distance d, assuming we use at least d rounds of stabiliser measurements. Un-branching by measuring out ancilla qubits and measuring all stabilisers in the original code is also a fault-tolerant operation, but only requires one round of stabiliser measurements.

Despite brute-force branching originally being defined for X or Z-type operators on a CSS code, it is possible on any stabiliser code under a suitable condition given below. This observation is similar to the approach in Ref. [39] for measurement, but for branching

Lemma 2.10. Let Q be a stabiliser code. Let I ={ ̄Λ1, ̄Λ2,··· , ̄Λt} be a set of t logical Pauli representatives such that for each i,j∈ [t] and data qubit α in Q either (a) ̄Λi and ̄Λj act on α with the same Pauli operator or (b) at least one of ̄Λi and ̄Λj act with identity on α. Then all t logical representatives can be simultaneously branched onto leaves. Proof. For each data qubit α in V = ⋃ i ̄Λi, apply a suitable single-qubit Clifford Cα to convert the logical representative into a Z Pauli on that qubit. This permutes the bases of incident checks accordingly. As the logical representatives act with the same Pauli, or the identity, this simultaneously changes the basis of every logical representative in I on data qubit α to Z or I. Now, every check on the code which locally anticommutes with the action of any ̄Λi on a given qubit α has a Yα or Xα term. Considering only the Xα component of a Yα term, construct the branch accordingly as for ̄Z logicals in a CSS code. Last, convert each data qubit back to the original basis by applying C† α. As the checks all commute in the Z basis, they must also commute when permuted back to their original basis. Because there exists a product of checks which cleans each logical ̄Λi to a leaf in the Z basis, the same product of checks must clean that logical to a leaf in the original basis. The basis changing is a step performed offline to compute the checks and connectivity required for the branches; the local Cliffords are not intended to be physically applied on

[AX|AZ] is the check matrix of the codeQ restricted to those checks withX-support inS1. Dangling edges are left on the l.h.s. to indicate connections to the rest of the code, and on the r.h.s. to indicate connections to the rest of the branch. There is a similar, overlapping branch for S2 ⊂ V . Observe that this S1 branch is identical to ̄Z logical branching in a CSS code, albeit some incident checks to S1 in the original code have some Z check component, because they involve measurements in the Y basis. This Z check component on the original code does not affect the commutation relations or multiplication of logical operators through to leaves by Z checks in odd layers. Because this more general branching is equivalent to branching ̄Z logicals up to local Cliffords and an irrelevantAZ check component on the original code, all previous lemmas from this section apply. Another consequence of this generalised branching is that each logical representative on a leaf will be a product of Z Paulis, regardless of the basis it acted on in the original code – whether it is a ̄Z, ̄X or ̄Y operator.

Our procedure for fault-tolerant quantum computation also involves gauging logical measurements [39]. Gauging logical measurements can be applied to any stabiliser code. In the case where a code is CSS the gauging logical measurement framework coincides with the homological measurement framework of Ref. [40]. Definition 2.11. [39] Let L be a ̄Z logical operator in a stabiliser code. A measurement of L in the gauging logical measurement framework uses a set of appended ancillary qubits and checks forming a graph G(V, E, F). G(V, E, F) has a set of vertices V, which are identified with Z checks, in 1-to-1 correspondence with data qubits of L. Each vertex has support on that data qubit in L given by the correspondence. G also has a set of edges E, which are identified with data qubits, and some of these are included in deformed X checks which are incident to L. Lastly, G has a set of faces F which form a cycle-basis of G. These faces are for gauge-fixing, are only connected to edges in E, and do not interact with the original code.

where L is the original logical operator, and S is the set of all X-checks incident to L. The sets V, E and F are newly introduced to perform the measurement, and • F is a matrix defining the connectivity from Z checks to data qubits in L; for our

• G is the incidence matrix of the graph G. • M defines the connectivity from X checks incident to L to new data qubits. M is determined by the choice of graph and initial logical operator. • N picks out a cycle basis of G, such that kerG = imN ⊺. To perform the measurement, initialise all new edges in G in the|+⟩ basis, and measure all stabilisers of the deformed code. The auxiliary graph G must satisfy some desiderata to yield a favorable code surgery

To ensure the deformed code has code distance at least the distance d of the original code, it is sufficient that 4. G has relative Cheeger constant βd(G,f(L))≥ 1. We elide the details of the expansion properties and perfect matchings, as they are not the focus of this work. It is sufficient for our purposes to say that, given any logical operator, these desiderata can always be satisfied, and in fact Ref. [50] proves that it is easy to do so.

The adapter edges joining auxiliary graphs Gl and Gr into one larger auxiliary graph are those hosting the qubits Q. The matrices Tl,Tr ,Pl,Pr are efficiently determined using the SkipTree algorithm, [45, Thm. 7]. We do not include in this diagram qubits or checks outside the supports of the logicals ̄Zl and ̄Zr , and instead suggest their existence through dangling edges. The space overhead of such a graph for measuring any arbitrary logical operator with weight O(ω) is O(ω log3 ω). The log3 ω factor comes from decongestion [44], whereby the graph is thickened in order to find a low-weight cycle-basis, a procedure which can be performed efficiently by a randomised algorithm. By thickening, we add “dummy vertices” which are not connected to the original code Q but are required to maintain the LDPC

Remark 2.13. The desiderata above ensure that the deformed code is LDPC when measuring only one target logical operator, or t disjoint logical operators. If there are many representatives to be measured, and they overlap substantially, then Theorem 2.12 is not sufficient to preserve the LDPC property, as data qubits at the overlap are involved in O(t)

Lemma 2.14. [39, Lem. 7] If all the desiderata of Theorem 2.12 are satisfied, the gauging measurement procedure given by initialising all new data qubits in suitable bases and measuring all stabilisers for at least d rounds of measurement has fault-distance d.

The last definition we need is that of adapters, whereby ancilla systems for measuring disjoint logical Paulis using the gauging logical measurements formalism can be connected to measure their product. Definition 2.15. [45] Consider two disjoint logical operators with accompanying graphs Gl and Gr defining gauging logical measurement systems for each individual operator. Then a universal adapter A is a set of additional vertices, edges and faces connected to Gl and Gr. This converts Gl and Gr into a larger, adapted graph Gl ∼A Gr. Theorem 2.16. [45, Thm. 11] Provided auxiliary graphs to perform gauging measurements of non-overlapping logical operators ̄Z0, ̄Z1,..., ̄Zt−1 that satisfy the graph desiderata of Theorem 2.12, there exists an auxiliary graph to perform gauging measurement of the product ̄Z0 ⊗ ̄Z1 ⊗...⊗ ̄Zt−1 satisfying the desiderata of Theorem 2.12.7 7The first version of this theorem required the logical operators to be irreducible but was later generalised to remove this requirement.

This gauging measurement first takes the set of operators ̄Z0, ̄Z1,..., ̄Zt−1 and applies adapters as in Figure 8 between t− 1 overlapping pairs of disjoint logicals, for example ̄Z0 ̄Z1 then ̄Z1 ̄Z2 etc., until all t logicals are connected. In particular, the measurement can be performed while maintaining the LDPC property and fault-distance of the code. This means that so long as we can separate logical operators to have disjoint support, we can perform Pauli product measurements of those operators freely. Importantly, the adapters add no further asymptotic overhead beyond that of gauging logical measurements, so if we have t Pauli terms in a logical product measurement we can measure products of them with O(tω log3 ω) space overhead. Remark 2.17. The gauging measurement can be applied directly to a product of disjoint logical operators, but in the worst case this achieves a less efficient scheme than using adapters. For a product of t terms with maximum representative weight ω, direct gauging logical measurements uses O(tω log3 tω) additional qubits, while employing adapters brings the qubit cost to O(tω log3 ω). Although the adapter scheme can also be viewed as a large gauging measurement, it structures the creation of the gauging measurement graph in such a way to reduce the space overhead. Unlike brute-force branching, we do not make use of the finer details of gauging logical measurements or universal adapters, and they can be considered black-box procedures for the purpose of our work. See Ref. [56] for a high-level overview of the construction of gauging logical measurements and adapters. 3 The parallel measurement procedure In this section we first consider only measuring single logical qubits of the same type (X or Z) in parallel on CSS codes. We then incrementally generalise this result to measurements in different bases including Y . In Section 3.4 we generalise to stabiliser codes. Then in Section 3.5 we show how to measure Pauli products in parallel, and in Section 3.6 we show how to measure arbitrary commuting sets of Pauli products. Definition 3.1 (Individual Pauli operator). Let Q be a quantum LDPC code, and let B = (C2)⊗k be a choice of tensor decomposition of the logical space L of Q into qubits, i.e. B ∼= L. Then an individual Pauli operator acts on a single copy of C2 in the tensor

In other words, an individual Pauli operator ̄Pi acts on only one logical qubit of Q. Clearly, this notion is basis-dependent: if a different basis is chosen, the same physical operator on the code could act on multiple (or different) logical qubits. Definition 3.2 (Pauli product). Let Q be a quantum LDPC code, and let B = (C2)⊗k be a choice of tensor decomposition of the logical space L of Q into qubits, i.e. B ∼= L. Then a Pauli product may act on multiple copies of C2 in the tensor decomposition. A Pauli product can then be expressed as ⨂ i∈[k] ̄Pi for individual Pauli operators ̄Pi. Each ̄Pi in a Pauli product is called a Pauli term, or just term, if it is clear from context. 3.1 Individual logicals of the same type We first consider the simple case where we have many logical qubits in a CSS code to measure simultaneously in the same basis, either Z or X. For example, measuring ̄Z1 and ̄Z2 simultaneously. We call these Z-type measurements, and similarly for X-type

The method first uses brute-force branching, then unlike in Ref. [46] the measurements on leaves are performed using expander graphs [39] rather than hypergraph products [28]. We illustrate this procedure in Figure 9. Lemma 3.3. Let Q be a CSS quantum LDPC code. We can simultaneously measure individual Pauli operators of the same type (Z or X), with representative weight at most ω, ont different logical qubits ofQ while retaining fault-distanced and the LDPC property, using O(tω(logt + log3 ω)) new data qubits and checks. Proof. Perform brute-force branching on the logicalsvi ∈ I, using the unionV of support on data qubits. Next, we use gauging logical measurements, appending expander graphs to the leaves of the brute-force branching tree, measuring each of the individual logicals we desire to measure. Any logicals which we do not wish to measure, but that are contained in V , are not fully branched, so are left without a leaf or appended expander graph. By a combination of Lemmas 2.9 and 2.14, this procedure is fault-tolerant with faultdistance d, assuming the brute-force branching step and measurement step are each performed for d rounds of stabiliser measurements. The brute-force branching process requires O(tω logt) additional qubits, and the gauging logical measurement a further O(tω log3 ω), resulting in a scaling O ( tω(logt+log3 ω) ) . We next consider measuring single logical qubits in parallel, but where the measurement bases are a mixture of Xs and Zs. For this we need to branch both ̄X and ̄Z operators at the same time. 3.2 Individual logicals of CSS type Lemma 3.4. Let Q be a CSS quantum LDPC code. Let the unions of ̄Z and ̄X logical representatives to be measured have no overlap, i.e. no ̄Z representative to be measured intersects with any ̄X representative to be measured. We can simultaneously measure individual Pauli operators with representative weight at most ω of either Z or X type on t different logical qubits on Q while retaining fault-distance and the LDPC property, using O(tω(logt + log3 ω)) new data qubits and checks. Proof. As each ̄Z logical has no intersection with an ̄X logical, each union of ̄Z and ̄X logicals can be branched independently, and their representative copies on leaves measured by gauging logical measurement. Formally, we can apply local Cliffords to each ̄X logical to convert it into a product of Z Paulis, and compute the branching of all t logicals as though they are ̄Z logicals using Lemma 2.10, then apply local Cliffords to convert back, to acquire a valid branching for the logicals of mixed types. Hence we can apply

Unfortunately, representatives of ̄Z and ̄X operators will generally overlap substantially, even when they commute. When the representatives overlap, the new checks introduced in Z-type and X-type branches do not commute in general, as the ̄X logicals are deformed when branching ̄Z logicals and vice versa [46, App. F]. Thus Lemma 3.4 requires the representatives to be chosen such that no ̄Z representative to be measured overlaps with any ̄X representative to be measured. This is always possible when the logical operators are on different logical qubits, as stated by the following lemma.

Figure 9: Branching and gauging measurement for two ̄Z logicals. Note that for just two logicals, branching is unnecessary and the gauging measurement systems can be appended in-place, but this scalable Tanner graph generalises to an arbitrary number of overlapping ̄Z logicals.

Lemma 3.5. Consider a CSS codeQ with check matricesHX,HZ and parameters [[n,k,d]]. We can find ̄X logical operators x1,··· ,xk ∈ Fn 2 and ̄Z logical operators z1,··· ,zk ∈ Fn 2 of this code, such that|xi ∩zj| =δij. Here∩ denotes intersection as sets. Corollary 3.6. In this basis, any set of ̄X and ̄Z operators acting on different logical qubits have representatives such that their unions have no data qubit overlap. Remark 3.7. We consider this lemma a standard result for CSS codes and include a proof in Appendix C for completeness. We are aware of independent proofs from [61], see Refs. [62, Sec. 4] and [63, Sec. 6]. It is also a special case of the ‘standard form’ for stabiliser codes given in Ref. [49, Sec. 4.1]. Remark 3.8. This choice of basis may give logical operators with substantially greater representative weight than the minimal weight possible for each logical operator. Lemma 3.5 gives an upper bound on the representative weight of a ̄Z logical of n−m−k + 1, so ω ∈ O(n) for LDPC codes. Similarly, the cleaned ̄X logical representatives may have larger weight than otherwise. Thus we emphasise that here ω is the largest weight of these chosen representatives, not the minimum available for each logical operator. Of course, while Lemma 3.5 shows that there exists a basis such that the unions of ̄Z and ̄X representatives do not overlap, there may be many such bases, and many valid choices of representatives with different weights; consider for example a surface code patch, which has only 1 logical qubit and many different representatives with different weights satisfying Lemma 3.5. Thus in practice it will be vital to determine low-weight representatives satisfying the no-overlap condition. Remark 3.9. For general quantum LDPC codes, finding a logical basis which possesses minimum-weight representatives is NP-hard [64], and hard to approximate [65], even without stipulating any further conditions such as the no-overlap condition above. Therefore, with general surgery schemes for logical measurement, even where the logical basis does not have conditions on its properties, one must be careful and compute the overheads in terms of ω, rather than assuming each representative has weight d. As an alternative option, rather than choosing new logical operators that satisfy the no-overlap condition, we could instead start with representatives that do overlap. Next, branch the ̄Z logicals, and track the overlapping ̄X logicals which are deformed by the branching. Then branch these ̄X logicals on top of the deformed code, so there will be some connectivity between the ̄X and ̄Z branches. When the ̄X logicals commute with every ̄Z logical contained in V = ⋃ ivi, the deformed ̄X logicals will pick up support in the branches with weight proportional to the number of checks required to clean them from V . When they do not commute with every contained ̄Z logical, which can happen if the logical operator basis is not the chosen basis given by Lemma 3.5, then they may pick up support on up to O(tω logt) new data qubits in the branches. As O(tω logt) is not bounded by O(n) in general, this can be far worse than choosing a suitable basis, but could be preferable at finite sizes. We discuss this further in Appendix E. 3.3 Individual logicals of non-CSS type We now consider the case when there are also ̄Y Paulis to be measured. Unlike in Ref. [46] we do not use ancilla logical qubits or additional codeblocks for this procedure. Instead, we use the same chosen basis as in Section 3.2.

Corollary 3.10. Let ̄Λi and ̄Λj be any two arbitrary Pauli operators – ̄X, ̄Y or ̄Z – on different logical qubits i, j with representatives given by Lemma 3.5. Let α be an arbitrary data qubit. Either (a) ̄Λi and ̄Λj act on α with the same Pauli operator or (b) at least one of ̄Λi and ̄Λj act with identity on α. As a consequence, given any set oft≤k logical Pauli operator representatives ̄Λ1, ̄Λ2,··· , ̄Λt from Lemma 3.5 ont different logical qubits, these can all be branched such that an equivalent logical operator appears on each leaf. Lemma 3.11. Let Q be a CSS quantum LDPC code, with a chosen basis of logical operators given by Lemma 3.5. We can simultaneously measure any Pauli operators on t different logical qubits individually on Q while retaining fault-distance and the LDPC property. Letting ω be the maximum representative weight of logicals to be measured, this

tω(logt + log3 ω) ) new data qubits and checks. Proof. First branch using Lemma 2.10. After branching, each representative is a product of Z Paulis on each leaf of the tree. Then use gauging logical measurements to measure each Pauli term on each leaf. By a combination of Lemmas 2.9 and 2.14 this operation is fault-tolerant with fault-distanced, given that the branching and measurement steps were each performed with at least d rounds of stabiliser measurements. 3.4 Individual logicals on stabiliser codes We now show that our protocol for measuring individual logical operators in parallel generalises to stabiliser LDPC codes which are not CSS codes. For this, we use the ‘standard form’ of stabiliser codes given in Ref. [49, Sec. 4.1]. Lemma 3.12. Let Q be a stabiliser quantum LDPC code, with a chosen basis of logical operators given by the ‘standard form’. Measuring logical Pauli products in parallel is a straightforward extension of the scheme outlined above to measure individual logical Paulis in parallel. The extension is straightforward because we can separate all logicals included in a set of parallel measurements onto disjoint supports by brute-force branching, and then applying universal adapters to the graphs introduced by the gauging measurement leaves Tanner graph connectivity unaffected elsewhere in the code, see Figure 10. Theorem 3.13. Let Q be a stabiliser quantum LDPC code, with a chosen basis of logical operators given by Lemma 3.5. We can simultaneously measure any logically disjoint Pauli products on t logical qubits on Q while retaining fault-distance and the LDPC property. Letting ω be the maximum representative weight of logical terms to be measured, this uses

tω(logt + log3 ω) ) new data qubits and checks. Proof. To measure Pauli products, we first repeat the procedure from Lemma 3.12, branching each logical operator term in each product and then performing gauging logical measurements. Now, we also introduce adapters between the measurement graphs for operators whose products are being measured. By Theorem 2.16 constructing adapters to make a single Pauli product preserves the desiderata of Theorem 2.12, and so fault-distance and the LDPC property. As each logical appears only once in any given product to be measured, by the assumption that we are measuring t terms on different logical qubits, there are at most two adapters connected to any measurement graph, so the LDPC property is preserved for arbitrary sized products. Similarly, each of the Pauli product measurements acts on disjoint sets of logicals, so the fault-distance of Lemma 2.14 carries through.

The same procedure for measuring logical Pauli products in parallel described above can be extended straightforwardly to the case where we measure logical Pauli products containing terms which have the same, or identity, action on every logical operator. In this case, the procedure is the same as for Theorem 3.13, except that when branching individual representatives to leaves we extend the branches (as depicted in Fig. 2d) to give multiple copies of each representative on different leaves. For example, if we wish to measure ̄X1 ̄Z2 ̄I3 simultaneously with ̄I1 ̄Z2 ̄X3, then we have four leaves in total: one for ̄X1, two for ̄Z2 and one for ̄X3. Therefore the space overhead of O ( Tω(logT + log3 ω) ) from Theorem 3.13 carries through, butT is now the number of non-identity terms in the set to be measured. To measure an arbitrary commuting set Θ of logical Pauli products in time independent of t, we cannot branch, say, ̄X1 at the same time as ̄Z1 in order to measure ̄X1 ̄Z2 ̄I3 simultaneously with ̄Z1 ̄X2 ̄I3. Therefore we instead use the technique of twist-free surgery from Ref. [48] to separate each Pauli product into a pair of commuting products which do not contain ̄Y terms, but do have additional support on logical ancilla qubits. While this is the same approach taken as in Ref. [46, App. H], we have two advantages. First, the overall space overhead of our scheme is lower as a consequence of using gauging logical measurements and universal adapters, rather than the CKBB scheme [28]. Second, this approach uses ancilla|Y⟩ states, which are potentially costly to prepare in the context of [46]. The authors proposed to either use a qLDPC code that supports a transversal S gate, or distil the|Y⟩ states which incurs an additional overhead. The parallel measurement protocol we have proposed can prepare all required|Y⟩ states in one measurement round. In other words, we bootstrap our measurement of arbitrary commuting sets off the ability of our scheme to measure Y operators without using|Y⟩ states. We now describe the procedure to measure arbitrary commuting products in more detail. We use the twist-free gadgets8 from Ref. [48], which first appeared in Ref. [66]. In such gadgets, we split up a product into two steps using ancillae. This uses the fact that any Pauli productP to be measured can be described asP =iu·vX[u]Z[v] for some binary vectors u and v defining the support of the X and Z components. If there are an even number of Y terms in P , so u·v is even, we initialise a single logical|0⟩ state on qubit A and split P into two products: X[u]XA and Z[v]XA. If there are an odd number of Y terms, so u·v is odd, we initialize one more logical|Y⟩ = 1√ 2 (|0⟩ +i|1⟩) state on qubit B, and split P into X[u]XAXB and Z[v]XAZB. This|Y⟩ state serves as a catalyst and is left unchanged by the measurements. These different cases are illustrated in Figure 11. Despite every product in Θ commuting, the decomposition above may produce products that anticommute. That anticommutation presents a problem for parallel measurements: we would like to measure all the X-type products in the same timestep, and then 8The terminology comes from the fact that Y basis measurements can be performed using “twists” in surface code patches. We are not using surface codes, but use the same terminology for consistency.

The measurement outcome of P is determined by the two split Pauli product measurements and the Z measurement. The|Y⟩ state in (c) is left unchanged. all the Z-type products. To ensure this does not happen, the operators in Θ must satisfy

Although [ ̄X1 ⊗ ̄Y2, ̄Z1 ⊗ ̄X2] = 0, [ ̄X1 ⊗ ̄X2, ̄Z1 ⊗ ̄I2]̸= 0, so the decompositions into X and Z-type products do not preserve commutation. As a consequence, the X-type products cannot be commuted through the Z-type products. Given a general set Θ of commuting Pauli product measurements, Θ may not be regular. However, observing that Θ forms a generating set for a group of Pauli products ⟨Θ⟩, it is shown in Ref. [46] that an alternative generating set Θ′∪ Θ′′ of⟨Θ⟩ can always be chosen such that the subsets Θ′ and Θ′′ are each regular. Measuring Θ′ and then Θ′′ then performs the same logical operation on the code as measuring Θ. We omit the details here, but refer the interested reader to [46, Lem. 9]. As this is a different set of Pauli product operators than Θ, the weights of the Pauli products in the set Θ′∪ Θ′′ may differ substantially from those in Θ. We then separate the measurement of our Pauli products into 4 steps:
